subject: QuantumHealth: reserve allocation & burst mitigation proposal
messages:
From: Monica Patel <monica.patel@redwood.ai>
To: Alex Zhou <alex.zhou@quantumhealth.com>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.ai>, Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwood.ai>, Priyom Das <priyom.das@redwood.ai>
Date: Mon, 18 Sep 2028 15:10:00 -0700
Subject: QuantumHealth: reserve allocation & burst mitigation proposal

Alex —

Thanks for the call today. Per our discussion, attached is a working capacity worksheet and an updated SLA draft (v2) that ties committed reserve to a burst pool and graceful degradation policies. High level summary below; details are in the worksheet.

Ask: confirm if QuantumHealth is comfortable with a 12-month reserved slab starting Nov 1, and whether procurement needs a shorter ramp window.

Supply-side assumptions and asks:
- Nominal workload: ~5,000 tokens/sec sustained (baseline product usage, 98th percentile hours).
- Peak design: up to 42,000 tokens/sec for short multi-hour surges (marketing events + nightly processing).
- Target SLO: p95 generation latency <= 300 ms for typical 1–2 turn chat requests (avg request size ~256 tokens).
- Preferred model: redwood-rlm-13b-q4 (mixed-quantized profile) for most production traffic; fallback path to redwood-rlm-7b-q4s for the highest concurrency tails.

Preliminary sizing (back-of-envelope):
- Measured throughput on our Dedicated A100-80GB profile: ~2,200 tokens/sec per GPU with batch=16 and avg seq=256 for the 13B quantized variant.
- Sustained GPUs required = ceil(5,000 / 2,200) => 3 GPUs (rounded to a 4-GPU reserved slab to avoid tight packing).
- Peak GPUs for surge (no shared burst pool) = ceil(42,000 / 2,200) => 19 GPUs.
- Recommended reserved commit: 12 GPUs dedicated (gives ~26,400 tokens/sec sustained capacity) + burst pool of 10 GPUs shared regionally to absorb peaks, plus model fallback logic. That gives roughly 40–45% headroom on sustained traffic and room to absorb multiple concurrent peaks.

Operational mitigations included in the worksheet:
- Adaptive routing: route non-latency-sensitive batch jobs to lower-cost quantized nodes.
- Prefix/KV caching for repeated prompt patterns (expected to reduce effective tokens/sec by ~12% for backend inference).
- Canary rollouts and automatic model fallbacks (13B -> 7B) if tail latency exceeds 400 ms for 5 consecutive minutes.

Attachments: capacity worksheet (spreadsheet) and SLA (pdf).

Next step: if these numbers look directionally correct, Ben and Priyom can produce a formal GPU-slab plan with per-hour cost and a canned runbook for surge absorption. Happy to hop on a call with procurement next week.

Best,

Monica Patel
Senior Account Executive | Redwood Inference

Monica —

Appreciate the quick turnaround and the worksheet. A couple of clarifying Qs before we take this to procurement:
1) When you say 2,200 tokens/sec per A100-80GB, what measured distribution (seq length / batch / sampler) was that based on? Our traffic has a bimodal distribution: ~65% short chats (~40 tokens) and ~35% long document generation (avg 1,200 tokens). How does that change the numbers?
2) The proposed 12 GPU reserved + 10 GPU burst model looks reasonable from a headroom perspective, but procurement will ask for ramp phasing (months 0–3, 4–6, 7–12) and potential credits if we downgrade reserved levels mid-contract.
3) For p95 <= 300ms: is that measurable across geo fallback (we will be multi-region), and do you expect cold-cache warmups to cause SLO blips during the first 2 hours of a campaign surge?

Can we get a scenario breakdown showing: steady-state, single simultaneous peak (marketing event), and concurrent peaks (marketing + nightly batch + partner spikes)?

Thanks — looping in procurement.

Alex — Monica —

Quick technical breakdown to answer the distribution question and give the scenario table Alex requested. I pasted the key math from our bench runs below. All numbers assume our Dedicated runtime with KV caching enabled unless noted.

Bench assumptions (redwood-rlm-13b-q4 on A100-80GB, batch tuning enabled):
- short-chat profile (avg seq 40 tokens, batch 32): ~6,800 tokens/sec per GPU (higher due to short seq, good batching).
- long-doc profile (avg seq 1,200 tokens, batch 4): ~520 tokens/sec per GPU (long kv propagation, lower throughput).
- blended, traffic-weighted throughput = 0.65*6,800 + 0.35*520 = 4,670 tokens/sec per GPU. We conservatively used 2,200 as a safe sustained estimate on aggregated mixed traffic to account for variability, warmup, and tail effects.

Scenario sizing (rounded up to nearest whole GPU slab; reserve/burst split recommended):
- Steady-state (our baseline 5,000 tokens/sec):
  * Using blended per-GPU 4,670 tps -> ceil(5,000/4,670) = 2 GPUs.
  * Safety cushion + ops preference -> reserve 4 GPUs.
- Single marketing event (peak 42,000 tokens/sec, short-chat heavy):
  * For short-chat mode per-GPU = 6,800 tps -> ceil(42,000/6,800) = 7 GPUs.
  * If traffic flips to long-docs, required would be ceil(42,000/520) = 81 GPUs (impractical); therefore we recommend request-level queuing for very large long-doc jobs and scheduling them outside peak windows or routing to a separate batch pool.
- Concurrent peaks (marketing + nightly batch + partner spikes -> effective peak 62,000 tokens/sec blended):
  * Conservative blended per-GPU = 2,200 tps -> ceil(62,000/2,200) = 29 GPUs.

Recommended contract topology (what we propose to put in the worksheet):
- Reserve slab: 12 GPUs (sustained capacity ~56,040 tps using conservative 4,670 blended figure), giving ~1.5–2x buffer on steady patterns and room to run background batch jobs without impacting P95 for user-facing chat.
- Regional burst pool: 10 GPUs shared across the account (on-demand style with soft limits, paid from a committed credit pool). Bursts consumed from the pool will be metered and capped per-hour to limit cost exposure.
- Fallback policies: automatic downgrade of streaming fidelity or model switch to 7B if p95 > 400ms for > 5m; queued long-doc jobs moved to batch lane.

Tail/cold-start considerations:
- Cold-cache effect is most visible for large KV contexts and first-warm request; warmup script can pre-warm ~60% of expected KV entries within 10–30 minutes. We recommend a scheduled warmup run in the 2 hours leading up to any planned marketing surge (we can operate this as an add-on run during campaign prep windows).

Operational cost estimate (monthly, rough):
- Reserved 12 x A100-80GB equivalent: ~$168k/mo (committed discount assumed)
- Burst pool consumption (metered): variable; assume 10 GPUs consumed 10% of peak hours => ~$12k/mo incremental on average.

If QuantumHealth wants a staged ramp: Month 0–3 reserve 6 GPUs, Month 4–6 ramp to 10 GPUs, Month 7–12 settle at 12 GPUs. We can formalize credits if you expect to downscale mid-contract (typical 6–12% credit tiers for early termination / downscale events).

Happy to draft the scenario table into the worksheet and hand to procurement.

Ben Carter

Alex / Procurement team —

Thanks for the questions and the prompt review. Ben's breakdown should cover the distribution concerns — the key operational ask from QuantumHealth will be: where do you want long-doc heavy jobs to run? If you want them on the same reserved slab we need a larger commit or strict scheduling windows. If you can tolerate asynchronous batch windows for long-doc jobs we can keep the reserved commit much smaller.

Summary of proposed next steps:
1) I will update the worksheet with three ramp scenarios (conservative, staged ramp, aggressive) and include a month-by-month cost and credit table.
2) Priyom will produce a brief runbook for surge warmup (pre-warm script, KV warm percentage, recommend pre-warm timing).
3) Kimberly and I will schedule a procurement/finance call for Thurs next week to walk through contract language and credit terms.

If procurement needs a shortened initial term (6 months) with a 6-month option extension, we can model that and show credit tiers. I've added a DocuSign draft link in the worksheet folder — please treat it as draft until procurement confirms ramp schedule.

I'll follow up later today with the updated worksheet and a proposed time for the procurement call.

Best,

Monica Patel
